questions.q: Which of these correctly lists the five metadata lifecycle stages in order, per this lesson?
options: Capture, store, publish, maintain, retire
Publish, capture, retire, store, maintain
Store, maintain, capture, publish, retire
Capture, maintain, store, retire, publish
questions.explain: The lifecycle moves from creation (capture) through storage, visibility (publish), ongoing upkeep (maintain), to eventual deprecation (retire).

questions.q: According to this lesson, which stage of the metadata lifecycle is most commonly skipped?
options: Capture
Publish
Maintain
Store
questions.explain: Capture and publish get attention because skipping them is an obvious, visible failure (no glossary launched, or a hidden glossary). Maintain gets skipped because nothing visibly breaks the day an entry goes stale.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a stale glossary definition is worse than having no entry at all?
options: Because a wrong definition is still trusted by whoever reads it, actively misleading them
Because stale entries take up more storage space than no entry
Because having no entry is always illegal under data protection law
Because a wrong definition cannot be corrected once published
questions.explain: An entry with no definition at least signals 'ask someone' — a wrong definition gets trusted and used, which is actively worse.

questions.q: What should happen to a metadata entry when the thing it describes is deprecated or deleted, per this lesson?
options: It should be marked retired, not silently deleted, so historical references still resolve
It should be immediately and permanently deleted with no trace
Nothing — retired entries are automatically handled by the database engine
It should be converted into a new business glossary term automatically
questions.explain: Retiring (marking as no longer current) rather than deleting preserves the ability for historical references and audits to still resolve correctly.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which practical sign indicates the 'maintain' stage is being skipped?
options: An owner field pointing to someone who has left the company
A glossary entry has a definition at all
A table has more than one column
A data catalog exists somewhere in the organization
questions.explain: An outdated owner field, a missing or very old 'last reviewed' date, and a definition that no longer matches reality are all signs an entry has drifted without anyone maintaining it.
